title: Gen Z Lags on Key Life Milestones but Leads in Retirement Saving, Early Investing
detail:
Gen Z Lags on Key Life Milestones but Leads in Retirement Saving, Early Investing
Elizabeth Guevara
Sun, November 1, 2026 at 8:30 AM CST 3 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Gen Z is falling behind on many financial milestones, besides investing in the stock market and for retirement.
Credit: Getty Images
KEY TAKEAWAYS

Generation Zers have a spending-to-savings ratio that's higher than that of older generations.

Gen Z is also delaying major milestones like homeownership and having children due to rising costs and slower wage growth.

However, Gen Zers are investing in the stock market and saving for retirement earlier than previous generations.

Young adults may be more inclined to buy themselves a "little treat," even at the cost of savings. But they're investing for the future earlier than previous generations.

Generation Z adults (those born between 1997 and 2008) have the lowest savings-to-spending ratio of any generation, according to a Bank of America report. Young adults without a college degree face the highest unemployment rate of any group of workers, at 7.2%. The unemployment rate for young adults with a college degree has also risen, from 4.2% three years ago to 5.7% in June, with many recent graduates struggling in the labor market.

Yet many Gen Zers have kept spending on small indulgences—makeup, coffee—even as inflation and unemployment have climbed.

"For Gen Z, this trend is consistent with the 'little treat economy,' where smaller discretionary indulgences remain appealing and might even be worth spending more on when larger financial milestones feel harder to reach," Bank of America's researchers said.

Why This Matters

Even as they're often putting off buying a home and raising children, Gen Zers are investing earlier than previous generations did. Starting young gives their money more time to compound, which means more wealth by the time they need it.

Gen Zers entered adulthood as the cost of many monthly expenses rose faster than wages, making it harder to reach the middle class.

Home prices have risen about 210% since 2000, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency's house price index. Raising children has grown more costly, as childcare and school costs have climbed nearly 190% since 2000. Meanwhile, wages have grown by only about 84% over the same period.

More than three in 10 Gen Zers say money problems have pushed back their plans to buy a home, and a quarter say the same about having children, according to Northwestern Mutual's 2026 Planning & Progress survey.

While fewer young Americans are buying homes and more of them rely on help from their families to afford a down payment, Gen Zers are ahead of previous generations in investing.

In 2024, 37% of 25-year-olds had moved significant money from checking into an investment account since turning 22, according to the JPMorganChase Institute. In 2015, just 6% had.

Bank of America's top strategist has found value in an unloved corner of the AI trade: the bonds of the companies paying for it.

"Buy tech bond 'diamonds-in-rough' as AI hyperscalers up equity issuance, cut buybacks," Michael Hartnett, chief investment strategist at Bank of America, said in his latest Flow Show note.

The call comes after a punishing year for tech credit.

Why Hartnett Calls Tech Bonds 'Diamonds in the Rough'

According to Hartnett, U.S. technology bonds have lost about 9% so far in 2026.

That leaves their total return relative to the broad investment-grade bond index at the lowest level in 30 years. In other words, tech debt has rarely looked this cheap compared with the rest of the high-grade market.

The main reason is supply. AI hyperscalers have sold $182 billion of bonds this year, up from just $17 billion in 2024, as they borrow to build data centers.

Investors have demanded higher yields to absorb that wave. As a result, long-dated bonds of the Magnificent Seven and other AI leaders now yield between 6% and 8%, a level Hartnett considers attractive.

Why Bondholders Are Gaining the Upper Hand

The second part of Hartnett's argument concerns how the hyperscalers are now raising money.

Meta's recent share sale, he said, signals a new respect for credit investors. Selling stock rather than adding more debt strengthens the balance sheet that bondholders rely on.

Hartnett also believes the long stretch in which AI bonds lagged AI stocks is coming to an end.

Hyperscalers have raised $89 billion through equity issuance in 2026. At the same time, their share buybacks are running at an annualized pace of just $14 billion, down from $105 billion in 2024.

title: What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
detail:
What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 8:35 AM CDT 5 min read
MA
BAC
JPM
C
COF
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Credit cards are a huge benefit and a huge risk because they make it easy to spend. And since you don't have to pay the bill for 30 days or so, the hit can sometimes take consumers by surprise. This is why you can get an important read on consumers by looking at the credit card businesses of large banks like Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Citigroup (NYSE: C), and Capital One (NYSE: COF). The read after the third quarter: the consumer is looking good. Here's the proof.

Banks take on the credit risk

While credit cards usually carry the logos of companies like Visa (NYSE: V) or Mastercard (NYSE: MA), those companies are just payment processors. They charge small fees for facilitating financial transactions; the banks that issue the credit cards bear the financial risk. If a customer doesn't pay their credit card bill, banks like Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Capital One have to eat the cost.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

That said, issuing credit cards can be a very profitable business. So there's a balance that has to be struck between risk and reward. And when it comes to the risk side, banks tell you each quarter what's going on. They do this by reporting their 30-day and 90-day delinquency ratios and charge-off ratios. You just have to dig into the financial releases to find the data.

Everything is OK for now

Citigroup's credit card operations had a 30-day delinquency ratio of 1.16% in its own branded card portfolio in the third quarter. In cards it issues for other companies, often called private-label cards, that ratio was 1.96%. Private-label cards tend to be issued to riskier customers. Still, neither figure is particularly bad, and both are lower than they were a year ago. That same story holds for the 90-day delinquency ratios, which came in at 1.21% for Citigroup's cards and 1.92% for private-label cards.

JPMorgan Chase is the same exact story. The fairly strong 1.97% 30-day delinquency rate was down from a year ago. And the even stronger 90-day delinquency rate of 0.96% was also down from a year ago.

Bank of America's story is no different. Its 30-day delinquency rate stood at 2.32% in the third quarter of 2026, down from the same quarter in 2025. Its 90-day delinquency rate was 1.13%, also down year over year. That said, the company also reports net charge-offs, which came in at 3.22%. Like the delinquency rates, the financial giant's charge-offs were lower than they were a year ago.

Key Takeaways

Bank of America cut its DoorDash price target to $257 from $275 on Oct. 30 but kept its Buy rating. That target is 44% above a stock that's down 33% in a year.

In the third quarter, DoorDash reported record revenue and profit. It also agreed to buy Instacart for about $17 billion, at least 75% of it in cash.

DoorDash trades at 25x forward earnings, its lowest in five years, and Bank of America's target implies 35x, below the stock's three-year average.

Bank of America's call looks right on the numbers. The risks are the debt and new shares from the Instacart deal and how long it will take to close.

DoorDash (DASH:NASDAQ) just reported record revenue and profit, and agreed to buy Instacart (CART:NASDAQ) for about $17 billion. Its stock is still down 33% from a year ago, at $179 as of Thursday's close.

On Oct. 30, Bank of America analyst Justin Post cut his price target to $257 from $275 and kept his Buy rating. That's 44% upside.

A year of bigger bills

The trouble started in November 2025, when management said it would spend several hundred million dollars more in 2026 on new projects.

That bill showed up in the second quarter of 2026, when diluted EPS fell to $0.46 from $0.65.

Then, on Oct. 29, came a much bigger bill: Instacart at $65 a share, at least 75% in cash.

Bank of America is still a buyer

Post's $257 target matches the Street's average to the dollar, and the quarter backs him up. Third-quarter revenue rose 34% to $4.6 billion, net income jumped 91% to $466 million, and adjusted EBITDA climbed 41% to $1.06 billion, in the top half of management's guidance.

The Street's average target has fallen from $303 a year ago to $257:

Targets run from $172 to $350, and 43 analysts cover the stock.

Analysts cut their 2026 and 2027 normalized EPS estimates over the past year, but they've raised both by 5% to 6% since June 30. They now expect normalized EPS to climb from $5.10 in 2025 to $8.25 in 2027 and $10.16 in 2028:

The quarter's beat should help the 2026 and 2027 estimates hold up. The 2028 estimate is harder to call, since DoorDash plans to reinvest more than all of the Instacart synergies in the first year after closing.

At [$179], DoorDash trades at 25x forward earnings, its lowest in five years. Post's $257 works out to 35x expected earnings over the next twelve months. That's above the stock's one-year average of 33x and below its three-year average of 39x.

All three main equity indexes gapped down at Friday's open, as the rotation out of technology and artificial intelligence infrastructure accelerated to a frightful pace on All Hallows Eve. Investors, traders and speculators are seeking safety in energy, consumer staples and healthcare stocks, as well as Treasury bonds, amid rising concern about capex plans and return on AI.

By the closing bell, the Nasdaq Composite had fallen 2.9% to 25,437, the tech-heavy index's steepest single-day decline since March 2025, turning what had been a modest weekly gain into a 2% weekly loss.

The broad-based S&P 500 was off 1.8% at 7,580, resulting in a 0.6% decline for the week. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.1% today to 51,770. Papa Dow dipped 0.9% this week.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," LPL Financial Chief Cross-Asset Strategist Adam Turnquist observes. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."

Alphabet (GOOGL, -1.4%) reported its weakest ad revenue growth in five quarters, while e-commerce sales for Amazon (AMZN, -1.4%) slowed to a three-year low. But Microsoft (MSFT, -1.6%) reported a nice pop for cloud revenue, including expectations-beating Azure sales.

Still, according to Turnquist, the Magnificent 7 stocks are showing signs of weakness from a technical perspective.

Indeed, the Magnificent Seven Index has broken below support near its May highs and is approaching another key level. Relative strength "is also at a critical inflection point," with more deterioration from here suggesting leadership "is rotating away from mega-cap stocks."

The wider technology complex was also destabilized on Friday by a reported $6.3 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance engineered by agents of North Korea's government.

Intel is way outside

Intel (INTC, -28.6%) was the worst S&P 500 stock on Friday after management reported mixed results and offered weak guidance, amid a more-rapid-than-anticipated deceleration for its core PC market.

The chipmaker expects to report earnings of 25 cents per share for the fourth quarter on revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion. Wall Street forecast EPS of 45 cents on revenue of $17.3 billion.

Reddit's (RDDT) Q3 user miss was driven by weaker search-referral traffic, which declined further in October, with current trends pointing to a low-double-digit decline in daily active users in Q4, BofA Securities said Friday in a note.

Reddit's Q3 revenue was $895 million, exceeding Street estimates. Q3 daily active users were 130.3 million, below the Street consensus, driven by a decline in Google search referral traffic, according to the note.

The company is shifting marketing spend toward app installs and plans to test a logged-in-only experience internationally in Q4, BofA noted. The firm expects the transition to a logged-in user experience to take multiple quarters and weigh on headline traffic trends, the note added.

However, the change could result in a higher quality user base, improve monetization and eliminate the Google traffic overhang, the brokerage said. BofA expects sentiment to remain subdued for a few quarters until Reddit demonstrates positive growth momentum for US logged-in users.

BofA kept a neutral rating on Reddit and lowered its price target to $135 from $190.

Shares of Reddit were down 26% in Friday trading.
